questions.stem: What defines two substances as allotropes of each other?

options.text: They contain the same element bonded in different arrangements
options.explanation: Carbon's diamond and graphite are the classic pair.

options.text: They contain the same atoms in the same arrangement
options.explanation: Identical arrangements would be the same substance.

options.text: They contain different elements with similar properties
options.explanation: Allotropes are single-element substances.
The difference is structural and physical, not cosmetic.

questions.stem: Why do giant covalent lattices melt at very high temperatures?

options.explanation: No ions roam these neutral networks.

options.text: A large number of strong covalent bonds must be broken throughout the structure
options.explanation: Melting means dismantling bonds across the whole network.

options.text: Weak intermolecular forces hold them together
options.explanation: Weak forces characterise simple molecules, not giant lattices.
Mass is not the mechanism; bonding is.

questions.stem: Which property distinguishes graphite from diamond in terms of electrical behaviour?

options.explanation: Their electron availability differs.
Graphite's delocalised electrons carry current.
Graphite's spare electron roams the layers; diamond's electrons are all bonded.
The conductive member is graphite.

questions.stem: Diamond and silicon(IV) oxide are both hard because

options.text: their atoms slide easily over each other
options.explanation: Easy sliding makes graphite soft, the opposite case.
They melt very high.

options.text: they contain free electrons that stiffen them
options.explanation: Neither has free electrons; stiffness comes from bonded networks.

options.text: their 3D covalent networks are extremely hard to snap
options.explanation: Hardness reads the strength and continuity of the network.

questions.stem: Graphite is soft because

options.text: the forces between its carbon layers are weak and easily overcome
options.explanation: Layers shear off despite strong in-layer bonding.

options.text: its covalent bonds are individually weak
options.explanation: In-layer covalent bonds are very strong.

options.text: it contains no covalent bonds at all
options.explanation: Every carbon bonds covalently to three neighbours.

options.text: its atoms are arranged in 3D tetrahedra
options.explanation: That describes diamond.

questions.stem: Define allotropes.
questions.modelAnswer: Allotropes are substances containing only one element whose atoms bond in different arrangements, giving completely different physical properties.

questions.stem: State why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Graphite has delocalised electrons between its carbon layers that move along the layers under a voltage; diamond's four outer electrons per atom are all locked in covalent bonds, leaving none free.

questions.stem: Explain why the same element can produce both the hardest and one of the softest natural substances.
questions.modelAnswer: Property follows arrangement, not ingredient: diamond ties every atom into a rigid 3D covalent network, while graphite ties atoms only within sheets and lets the sheets rest on weak interlayer forces, so one scratches and the other shears.

questions.stem: A lab drawer holds two black pencils 'lead' samples, one conducting and one insulating when tested along the same axis. Assign each to its allotrope and justify.
questions.modelAnswer: The conducting sample is graphite - its delocalised electrons run along the layers - and the insulating one is diamond dust, whose electrons are all committed to four covalent bonds with no spare carrier.

questions.stem: How many other carbon atoms does each carbon touch in graphite?

options.explanation: Each atom touches three neighbours, not six.
The fourth outer electron stays free.
That is diamond's arrangement.
Graphite forms hexagonal sheets.

questions.stem: What gives graphite its electrical conductivity?

options.explanation: Weak forces enable sliding, not conduction.
Geometry without free electrons conducts nothing.

options.text: Free electrons that migrate along the layers carrying charge
options.explanation: One spare electron per atom moves under a voltage.
No ions exist in graphite.

questions.stem: Why do graphite's layers slide over each other so easily?

options.text: The covalent bonds within layers are weak
options.explanation: They are very strong.
Conduction and lubrication are separate effects.
Attraction, weak but real, holds them.

options.text: Weak van der Waals' forces between layers are easily overcome
options.explanation: The strong in-layer bonds stay intact while sheets shear.

questions.stem: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form?

options.explanation: All four outer electrons are committed.
That is graphite's ledger.
Two bonds would strand the octet.
Eight neighbours exceeds carbon's bonding capacity.

questions.stem: Which statement about diamond's bonds is correct?

options.text: Its bonds break easily under pressure
options.explanation: Diamond is the hardness benchmark.

options.text: All the covalent bonds are identical and very strong, with no intermolecular forces present
options.explanation: A uniform 3D network with nothing weaker inside.

options.text: Alternate bonds are strong and weak
options.explanation: Diamond's bonds are all identical.
No intermolecular forces exist in the network.

questions.stem: State the bonding arrangement of graphite, including bond count and structure shape.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon atom bonds to three others, forming layers of hexagons, with one free electron per atom left over.

questions.stem: State the bonding arrangement of diamond and its consequence for electrical conduction.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon bonds to four others in a tetrahedron; with every outer electron in a covalent bond, there are no freely moving electrons and diamond does not conduct.

questions.stem: Explain why graphite's in-layer strength and interlayer weakness coexist.
questions.modelAnswer: Within a sheet, each carbon invests three strong covalent bonds in its neighbours, but between sheets only weak van der Waals' attractions operate, so the same crystal is brutal to stretch and effortless to shear.

questions.stem: Predict which allotrope suits both an electrical contact and a dry lubricant, and explain the shared structural reason.
questions.modelAnswer: Graphite serves both: the same delocalised electrons that carry current along layers belong to a structure whose weakly held layers slide under shear - one arrangement, two applications.

questions.stem: What exactly is graphene?

options.text: A spherical network of carbon atoms
options.explanation: That describes fullerenes.
That describes diamond.

options.text: A single layer of graphite - one continuous hexagonal carbon sheet
options.explanation: The definition of record for the material.

options.text: A stack of many graphite layers
options.explanation: Stacks are graphite itself.

questions.stem: Why is graphene described as a 2D molecule?

options.explanation: Conduction is a consequence, not the definition.
Flatness of the ring is incidental; the sheet's thickness is the point.
Its atoms are covalently bonded throughout.

options.text: It is only one atom thick
options.explanation: Thickness vanishes at the atomic limit.

questions.stem: Which applications does the note assign to graphene?

options.explanation: Its unusual properties serve both fields.
Those are bulk graphite applications.
That is diamond's niche.
Neither appears in the graphene material story.

questions.stem: How does graphene's bonding compare with graphite's?

options.explanation: In-plane covalent bonds remain strong.

options.text: Identical per-atom bonding - three covalent bonds in a hexagonal sheet - just without the stacked layers
options.explanation: Graphene is one graphite layer isolated.

options.text: Four bonds per atom like diamond
options.explanation: Graphene keeps graphite's three-bond ledger.
Both are pure carbon.

questions.stem: A researcher peels successive layers from graphite until reaching one layer. Which property difference should they expect?

options.text: The sheet becomes harder than diamond
options.explanation: No such claim holds.
The dimensional change is the whole point.

options.text: The final single sheet still conducts along its plane but no longer benefits from layer sliding
options.explanation: In-plane electronics remain; the interlayer feature vanishes with the stack.

options.text: The sheet loses its conduction entirely
options.explanation: Graphene retains in-plane conduction.

questions.stem: State the structural definition of graphene.
questions.modelAnswer: Graphene is a single layer of graphite: a sheet of carbon atoms covalently bonded into one continuous hexagonal layer.

questions.stem: State the two application areas named for graphene.
Explain why graphene's single-sheet structure gives it unusual properties compared with bulk graphite.
questions.modelAnswer: All of graphite's interlayer behaviour - sliding, weak van der Waals failure planes - disappears at one atom thick, leaving a pure 2D covalent membrane whose electron behaviour and strength are unlike any bulk material.

questions.stem: A composite engineer wants a conductive, one-atom-thin additive for a polymer film. Choose the allotrope and give the two structural facts that justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Graphene: it is one continuous hexagonal carbon sheet (so one atom thin) and its per-atom free electron conduction runs along the sheet, exactly what a conductive additive needs.
